harder.brainstorming: The question has already survived three attempts requiring architectural pattern matching, full-cycle capability verification, and multi-dimensional similarity disambiguation—all passed. The system successfully retrieves papers sharing subsets of AI Scientist v2's properties and correctly categorizes them. To make this harder, I need to exploit a weakness the system hasn't faced yet. One option: force temporal reasoning about whether retrieved 'similar' systems were actually predecessors, contemporaries, or successors to AI Scientist v2, requiring the system to check publication dates and recognize that many 'similar' systems might postdate AI Scientist v2 and therefore represent derivatives rather than independent comparable work. Another option: require the system to identify which papers AI Scientist v2 itself cites as related work versus which are merely keyword-similar, forcing it to distinguish author-acknowledged similarity from retrieval-based similarity. The strongest option exploits that the system can retrieve both AI Scientist v1 (2024) and v2 (2025) but struggles with counterfactual reasoning: ask which papers would remain relevant if AI Scientist v2 had NOT introduced tree search, forcing the system to subtract out tree-search-specific papers and reason about what core capabilities remain necessary.
harder.chosen_strategy: Require counterfactual reasoning about capability dependencies. The question will ask which papers remain relevant to AI Scientist v2 if a specific architectural innovation (tree search) had never been introduced, forcing the system to reason about which retrieved papers' relevance depends specifically on tree search versus which address more fundamental capabilities that any automated research system would need. This requires recognizing dependency relationships between capabilities rather than just listing papers with overlapping features.
harder.updated_question: If AI Scientist v2 had used iterative refinement instead of tree search, which papers addressing its other core capabilities—automated experiment execution, LLM-driven hypothesis generation, or computational peer review—would remain architecturally relevant?
harder.why_harder: The system must perform counterfactual reasoning: identify which retrieved papers' relevance depends specifically on the tree-search architecture versus which address capabilities orthogonal to search strategy. This requires understanding dependency relationships between system components (e.g., 'this paper's tree-search pruning technique becomes irrelevant, but its experiment-execution framework does not'). A retrieval-strong system may list all papers matching 'automated experiment execution' or 'LLM hypothesis generation' without recognizing that some are only relevant BECAUSE they also use tree search (e.g., papers about tree-search-specific evaluation metrics or tree-node-selection strategies), while others address capabilities any automated research system needs regardless of search method.
harder.verification_criterion: The answer must explicitly identify at least one paper it retrieved as NO LONGER relevant because its contribution is tree-search-dependent (citing evidence of tree-search-specific techniques like MCTS node selection, branch pruning, or tree-structured rollouts), and for each paper it claims REMAINS relevant, must cite evidence that the capability it addresses (experiment execution, hypothesis generation, or peer review) is described in a tree-search-independent way. Fails if it lists all retrieved papers as remaining relevant without excluding any tree-search-dependent contributions, or if it does not provide source-backed evidence distinguishing tree-search-independent versus tree-search-dependent techniques for its relevance judgments.

attempts.answer:
Below is a structured assessment of which papers addressing AI Scientist v2’s core capabilities (automated experiment execution, LLM‑driven hypothesis generation, and computational peer review) would remain architecturally relevant if v2 had used iterative refinement instead of tree search. Where applicable, we highlight how the capability layers map to search-agnostic stacks versus search‑specific control logic.

Context and counterfactual
- AI Scientist v2 presented an end‑to‑end agentic pipeline that iteratively formulates hypotheses, designs and executes experiments, analyzes data, and autonomously authors manuscripts, explicitly leveraging a progressive agentic tree‑search managed by an experiment manager agent and adding VLM feedback to the AI reviewer loop; one fully autonomous manuscript was submitted to an ICLR workshop and achieved acceptance above the average human threshold <cite id="ca32f651-2">AI Scientist‑v2 iteratively formulates scientific hypotheses, designs and executes experiments, analyzes and visualizes data, and autonomously authors scientific manuscripts; it eliminates reliance on human-authored code templates, leverages progressive agentic tree-search managed by an experiment manager agent, and integrates a VLM feedback loop in the AI reviewer for iterative refinement; one manuscript exceeded the average human acceptance threshold at an ICLR workshop</cite>. 
- Prior surveys note that v1 relied on manually crafted code templates and linear exploration, while v2 reduced reliance on templates and adopted agentic tree search plus experiment management agents for multi‑round exploration; they also summarize that LLM‑generated ideas often underperform when implemented, motivating robust execution, evaluation, and review subsystems <cite id="ca32f651-0">Early systems such as AI Scientist (v1) demonstrate end-to-end automation but rely heavily on manually crafted code templates and largely linear exploration workflows; later approaches including AI Scientist‑v2 and Kosmos incorporate agentic tree search and experiment management agents enabling iterative and multi-round exploration; LLM-generated ideas tend to underperform after implementation, with growing similarity and diminished diversity</cite>. 
- Analyses of automated discovery search argue that linear search struggles to revisit and improve bad hypotheses, whereas tree‑based or evolutionary search mitigate this by enabling branching exploration; however, score‑based heuristics can bias toward well‑implemented modest hypotheses, underscoring the need for execution-aware feedback and careful search control under finite budgets <cite id="ca32f651-3">Scientific discovery is iterative; prior AI Scientist systems have produced new constructions and planned/ executed autonomous syntheses; scaling requires efficient search; linear search makes it difficult to revisit and improve a bad hypothesis; tree-based and evolutionary algorithms alleviate this but rely on score-based heuristics that can conflate execution quality with hypothesis quality</cite>.

What would change if v2 used iterative refinement instead of tree search
- Iterative refinement shifts planning from branching program/experiment trees to local, stepwise improvement with explicit feedback loops; in contrast to tree search’s expansion/selection of candidate branches, refinement emphasizes critique, repair, and re-execution of the current hypothesis/experiment, often with multi‑prompt or multi‑run evaluation to converge quality <cite id="ca32f651-3">Tree-based search allows revisiting and improving upon initial bad hypotheses; score-based heuristics can bias selection toward well-implemented hypotheses; this motivates iterative feedback-aware strategies that separate hypothesis quality from execution artifacts</cite>. 
- Regardless of search modality, the execution layer (running code, training models, instrument control, data capture, and analysis) and its reliability remain the core bottleneck; evaluations show that even advanced systems score poorly on execution-heavy benchmarks and that end‑to‑end AI Scientist systems often fail to execute rigorous experiments, reinforcing the need for execution orchestration and error handling rather than just search overhead <cite id="a750e1c2-0">The fundamental bottleneck for AI Scientists is implementation capability; LLMs perform poorly on execution-heavy benchmarks (e.g., 1.8% on PaperBench); a review of 28 papers by five AI Scientist systems shows they lack execution capabilities to perform rigorous experiments and produce high-quality papers</cite>. 
- Iterative refinement would likely integrate tightly with automated peer review and auditing (rubric alignment, role‑play reviewers, VLM‑assisted figure critique) to drive hypothesis revisions and experiment re-runs, whereas tree search already used VLM‑based feedback to refine figures and content structure <cite id="ca32f651-2">AI Scientist‑v2 enhances the AI reviewer component by integrating a VLM feedback loop for iterative refinement of content and aesthetics of the figures</cite><cite id="ca32f651-0">Automated review systems face blind spots (overemphasis on technical correctness, difficulty distinguishing fine-grained acceptance, susceptibility to sycophancy); AgentReview simulates diverse reviewer roles to mitigate these deficiencies</cite>.

Papers addressing automated experiment execution that remain relevant under iterative refinement
- Lab orchestration and protocol execution stacks decouple from whether the planner uses trees or iterative loops. Architectures that turn natural‑language prompts into validated, graph‑structured protocols, run them end‑to‑end across instruments, and recover from errors provide the execution substrate that iterative refinement can repeatedly call <cite id="98ba464d-1">An AI agent architecture integrated into Experiment Orchestration System (EOS) uses an agentic loop with automated validation and error correction to support the complete experimental lifecycle: creating protocols, running and monitoring protocols and closed-loop optimization campaigns, and analyzing results</cite><cite id="98ba464d-2">An AI agent integrates LLMs with laboratory orchestration to create, submit, monitor, and analyze protocols via a directed acyclic graph of tasks and parameters, reasoning about devices and constraints; evaluated with a 97% first-attempt protocol generation success and order-of-magnitude reductions in interface actions</cite>. 
- Experiment‑as‑code (EaC) stacks propose declarative, portable, composable experiment programs with static validation and cross‑site execution; these capabilities are independent of search strategy and provide the safety/observability layer that iterative refinement can rely on for re-execution and CI <cite id="98ba464d-3">Existing lab automation (LIMS/ELNs) automates components but doesn’t support end-to-end execution; EaC envisions a well-typed, lab-independent program with explicit dependencies, capability schemas, and execution semantics enabling static validation, deterministic compilation, and cross-site execution; cloud labs provide centralized interfaces drawing analogies to cloud computing</cite>. 
- Closed‑loop autonomous labs (e.g., A‑Lab, RoboChem, CRESt) demonstrate feedback‑driven campaign orchestration with online characterization and statistical optimization (including Bayesian optimization/evolutionary search), offering iterative execution environments that LLM‑driven agents can leverage whether refining via local stepwise updates or via search <cite id="98ba464d-0">Closed-loop, feedback-driven platforms including A-Lab, RoboChem, and CRESt integrate robotic execution with online characterization and statistical optimization (Bayesian optimization and evolutionary search), adapting parameters in response to observed outcomes over extended campaigns</cite><cite id="98ba464d-2">AI agent supports running and monitoring closed-loop optimization campaigns and analyzing results</cite>. 
- Broader surveys that decompose “automation of science” into protocol reasoning, tool invocation, training loops, and virtual labs reinforce that iterative refinement fits within L2‑S/L2‑I layers (single‑step or interactive workflow automation), where planning/revision is decoupled from execution orchestration <cite id="98ba464d-4">With the rise of language models, systems such as BioPlanner and LitLLM moved toward protocol reasoning and literature-centered support; in 2024, A‑Coscientist connected LLMs to search, code execution, documentation, and experimental automation; A‑Lab demonstrated autonomous materials synthesis via computation, knowledge, active learning, and robotic execution; 2024 systems extended bounded execution into planning, implementation, revision, and virtual experimental environments, forming L2‑S and L2‑I layers</cite>. 
- Critically, iterative refinement would still need robust error detection, rollback, and CI‑style gating (e.g., automated lab agents with validation and error correction) to ensure that repeated hypothesis revisions execute safely and reproducibly <cite id="98ba464d-1">Integrated into EOS, the AI agent operates under an agentic loop with automated validation and error correction, supporting complete experimental lifecycle and monitoring</cite>.

Papers on LLM‑driven hypothesis generation that remain relevant under iterative refinement
- AI Co‑Scientist and related systems focus on hypothesis generation via generation, debate, ranking, and evolution; these components provide the ideation and critique primitives that iterative refinement can reuse for local improvement cycles rather than global tree branching <cite id="a750e1c2-4">AI Co‑Scientist focuses on hypothesis generation using generation, debate, ranking, and evolution, adopted as a strong baseline pattern and tested with small combination pilots</cite><cite id="ca32f651-0">Later approaches such as AI Scientist‑v2 reduce reliance on explicit templates through agentic tree search and experiment management agents, enabling iterative and multi-round exploration</cite>. 
- Auditing question formation (FirstResearch) makes assumptions, mechanisms, tensions, and falsifying tests explicit, directly feeding iterative refinement loops that generate targeted revisions and experiments without broad search over hypotheses <cite id="98ba464d-4">FirstResearch focuses on the question-formation layer, forcing each candidate to expose primitive assumptions, mechanism, tension, and falsifying test, complementing workflow systems</cite>. 
- Surveys of embodied vs. language‑heavy systems emphasize that hypothesis‑driven inquiry requires maintaining structured relations among hypothesis, evidence, experiment, and revision—precisely the representation needed to drive iterative refinement cycles whether via search or via local critique and re‑execution <cite id="98ba464d-0">Language-heavy, action-light systems excel at execution but lack mechanism-aware reasoning and hypothesis-driven inquiry; structured science emphasizes maintaining relations among hypothesis, evidence, experiment, and revision</cite><cite id="98ba464d-4">Robot Scientist Adam demonstrated closed-loop automation generating hypotheses, designing experiments, executing them, and analyzing results; FirstResearch inherits this structured-science view but targets making the derivation of a proposed research question inspectable before execution</cite>. 
- Iterative search‑agnostic patterns like self‑consistency and multi‑prompt critique are already used to improve answer quality; in discovery agents, these map to multi‑run experiment evaluation and hypothesis polishing, so works on self‑critique/role‑play evaluation and rubric‑aligned feedback remain relevant to guide refinement <cite id="ca32f651-0">LLM reviewers exhibit blind spots; recent approaches such as AgentReview simulate diverse reviewer roles to mitigate deficiencies, though automated evaluation remains less reliable than human experts</cite>.

Papers on computational peer review that remain relevant under iterative refinement
- AI‑based referee agents and role‑play review frameworks (e.g., AgentReview) provide structured, diverse feedback; their mechanisms—rubric alignment, role specialization, and iterative critique—translate naturally into iterative refinement loops that propose targeted edits and re-runs of experiments and manuscript drafts <cite id="ca32f651-0">Recent approaches such as AgentReview simulate diverse reviewer roles to mitigate deficiencies in automated reviewers; automated evaluation systems remain less reliable than human experts in identifying robust accept/reject boundaries</cite><cite id="ca32f651-2">AI Scientist‑v2 integrates a VLM feedback loop to iteratively refine content and aesthetics of figures in the review stage</cite>. 
- Rubric‑aligned, retrieval‑augmented referee systems (e.g., GUIDE) provide structured, high‑fidelity scientific feedback and rubric modeling; these components decouple from search strategy and continue to inform hypothesis revision and experiment re‑planning under iterative refinement <cite id="ca32f651-4">A focused, retrieval-augmented, rubic-aligned system generates structured, high-fidelity scientific feedback</cite><cite id="a750e1c2-4">DeepReviewer-14B (Zhu et al., 2025) assesses 28 research papers generated by five AI Scientist systems, highlighting execution and quality gaps that peer-review-style feedback must address</cite>.

  - Computational peer review: referee agents, rubric‑aligned feedback, role simulation, and multimodal review loops to gate revisions and accept/reject decisions <cite id="ca32f651-0">AgentReview simulates diverse reviewer roles; automated reviewer deficiencies motivate robust referee loops</cite><cite id="ca32f651-4">Rubric-aligned, retrieval-augmented feedback yields structured, high-fidelity scientific review</cite><cite id="ca32f651-2">VLM-based iterative refinement of figures and content</cite>.

What would be less architecturally central if switching to iterative refinement
- Branch‑level search control and tree‑specific abstractions (e.g., node selection heuristics, tree expansion policies) become secondary; however, their diagnostics and reranking logic can be folded into iterative critique modules rather than core to the planner <cite id="ca32f651-3">Tree-based algorithms alleviate difficulties of linear search but rely on score-based heuristics that can bias selection toward well-implemented hypotheses</cite>.

Title: Idea2Story: An Automated Pipeline for Transforming Research Concepts into Complete Scientific Narratives
Snippet: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have driven growing interest in autonomous scientific discovery agents that aim to automate the full research lifecycle, from code generation to experimental execution (Hu et al., 2026;Zhang et al., 2025a;Lin et al., 2025). Early systems such as The AI Scientist (v1) (Lu et al., 2024) demonstrate the viability of end-to-end automation but rely heavily on manually crafted code templates and largely linear exploration workflows, which restrict discovery depth and adaptability. Later approaches, including The AI Scientist-v2 (Yamada et al., 2025) and Kosmos (Mitchener et al., 2025), reduce reliance on explicit template through the incorporation of agentic tree search and experiment management agents, enabling iterative and multi-round exploration. 

In research ideation, LLM-generated ideas are often perceived as highly novel during initial screening; however, prior studies (Si et al., 2024) uncover a critical paradox whereby such ideas tend to underperform after implementation relative to human-generated ideas, indicating limited feasibility and practical utility. As more ideas are generated, LLM outputs exhibit growing similarity, leading to diminished meaningful diversity. Similar limitations have also been observed in research evaluation and peer review (Liang et al., 2024;Xu et al., 2025;Thakkar et al., 2025;Zhang et al., 2026). Existing AI-based reviewers display systematic blind spots: Shin et al. (2025) shows that LLM reviewers place disproportionate emphasis on technical correctness while undervaluing novelty, deviating from human expert judgment, while Sahu et al. (2025) demonstrates that AI reviewers struggle to distinguish fine-grained acceptance categories and are susceptible to sycophancy, with review scores increasing unreasonably after exposure to author rebuttals. Although recent approaches such as AgentReview (Jin et al., 2024) seek to mitigate these deficiencies by simulating diverse reviewer roles, automated evaluation systems remain less reliable than human experts in identifying robust accept/reject decision boundaries.
</snippet>

Title: The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search
Snippet: AI is increasingly playing a pivotal role in transforming how scientific discoveries are made. We introduce The AI Scientist-v2, an end-to-end agentic system capable of producing the first entirely AI generated peer-review-accepted workshop paper. This system iteratively formulates scientific hypotheses, designs and executes experiments, analyzes and visualizes data, and autonomously authors scientific manuscripts. Compared to its predecessor (v1, Lu et al., 2024 arXiv:2408.06292), The AI Scientist-v2 eliminates the reliance on human-authored code templates, generalizes effectively across diverse machine learning domains, and leverages a novel progressive agentic tree-search methodology managed by a dedicated experiment manager agent. Additionally, we enhance the AI reviewer component by integrating a Vision-Language Model (VLM) feedback loop for iterative refinement of content and aesthetics of the figures. We evaluated The AI Scientist-v2 by submitting three fully autonomous manuscripts to a peer-reviewed ICLR workshop. Notably, one manuscript achieved high enough scores to exceed the average human acceptance threshold, marking the first instance of a fully AI-generated paper successfully navigating a peer review. This accomplishment highlights the growing capability of AI in conducting all aspects of scientific research. We anticipate that further advancements in autonomous scientific discovery technologies will profoundly impact human knowledge generation, enabling unprecedented scalability in research productivity and significantly accelerating scientific breakthroughs, greatly benefiting society at large. We have open-sourced the code at https://github.com/SakanaAI/AI-Scientist-v2 to foster the future development of this transformative technology. We also discuss the role of AI in science, including AI safety.
</snippet>

Title: Learning the ARTS of Search for Automated Discovery
Snippet: Scientific discovery is an iterative search process in which multiple hypotheses are proposed, tested, and refined to arrive at novel insights. The advent of large reasoning models have led to their use as AI Scientist conducting this search [36,31]. In the past, these systems have produced new constructions in extremal combinatorics [51], improved classical algorithms for matrix multiplication [39], planned and executed autonomous chemical syntheses [4], and generated novel hypotheses on antimicrobial resistance [15]. The success of these systems often rely on large sampling budgets and repeated execution of expensive experiments [51,39]. This cost is significant in ML research [50,38,7,53], where each hypothesis must be implemented as code, trained, debugged, and evaluated. Scaling automated research, therefore, requires efficient searching algorithms. 

Existing search algorithms fall into three categories: linear search, tree-based search, and evolutionary search. Searching linearly [38,20,31] makes it difficult for the agent to revisit and improve upon an initial bad hypothesis [42]. Tree-based [50,22,9,34,8] and evolutionary [39,44,33,52] algorithms alleviate this concern, but they search using score-based heuristics. This conflates hypothesis quality with it's execution in code. In such methods, a modest hypothesis that is well implemented is likely to be preferred over a promising hypothesis with preliminary execution. Through verbalized sampling the scientist then proposes diverse hypotheses with probabilities and samples one, which the executor implements, runs, and scores (Node expansion). Title: AI Scientists Fail Without Strong Implementation Capability
Snippet: The fundamental bottleneck for AI Scientists lies in their implementation capability to effectively execute the verification of these ideas. 

We defend our argument by analyzing quantitative evidence from existing benchmarks used to evaluate LLMs' abilities in performing complex engineering tasks (Section 3.2). While LLMs can generate highly novel ideas (Si et al., 2024, Chai et al., 2024, Gottweis et al., 2025), their performance in experiment execution is exceptionally poor (Table 1). For instance, a leading LLM like Claude 3.5 Sonnet scored only 1.8% on PaperBench (Starace et al., 2025). This implementation gap is further supported by a systematic evaluation (Section 3.3), which leverages a state-of-the-art review model, DeepReviewer-14B (Zhu et al., 2025), to assess 28 research papers generated by five advanced AI Scientist systems. The results demonstrate that current AI Scientist systems lack the execution capabilities needed to execute rigorous experiments and produce high-quality scientific papers. Finally, to clearly illustrate the root cause of the implementation gap, we provide an in-depth discussion on the fundamental limitations of AI Scientist (Section 4). 

In summary, this paper validates and deeply analyzes the implementation gap in existing AI Scientist systems based on extensive quantitative evidence and a simulated peer-review process. Furthermore, as the development of AI Scientists will bring greater regulatory challenges, we comprehensively examine the ethical considerations (Section 5) faced by AI Scientists and suggest directions for future research (Section 6). We hope this position paper will contribute to a clearer understanding of the limitations of current AI Scientist, shedding light on the future development of AI Scientist.
</snippet>

Title: The More You Automate, the Less You See: Hidden Pitfalls of AI Scientist Systems
Snippet: Automating the scientific enterprise has been an explicit research goal of computational and AI researchers for several decades [KRO + 09, SAB + 10, YLN22]. For instance, King et al. [KRO + 09] demonstrated the feasibility of fully automated systems for generating and testing scientific hypotheses, exemplified by the "Robot Scientist" capable of independently identifying functional genes in yeast metabolism. Sparkes et al. 

[SAB + 10] further advanced this line of work by integrating automated reasoning and laboratory robotics, aiming for autonomous scientific discovery with minimal human intervention. The advent of LLMs, along with their multimodal variants and agent-based extensions, has led to a surge in the development of automated scientist systems. We summarize several representative state-of-the-art systems in Table 1. 

There are different types of AI scientist systems, including those that are claimed to fully automate scientific discovery [LLL + 24, YLL + 25] and those designed to assist human scientists in their research [SSW + 25, Aut25, TZF + 25, Int25, GCM + 25]. Among the fully automated systems, The AI Scientist v1 [LLL + 24] is one of the earliest attempts to integrate the entire scientific pipeline: idea generation, code writing based on fixed templates, experiment execution, result visualization, manuscript drafting, and even simulated peer review. However, its reliance on pre-specified code templates and limited experiment management restricted flexibility. The AI Scientist v2 [YLL + 25] further eliminates the need for templates and introduces a treesearch-based experiment manager for more systematic exploration and incorporation of Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based feedback in the review stage. 

In contrast, in the case of AI assistants such as Carl [Aut25] and Zochi [Int25], human oversight is integral. Human experts must verify outputs at three checkpoints-transitioning from ideation to experimentation, from experimentation to presentation, and after presentation-before further progress is permitted. Agent Laboratory [SSW + 25] is designed to assist human scientists in executing their research ideas while allowing flexible levels of human involvement, where users can choose to provide feedback at any stage of scientific research.
</snippet>
<snippet id=a750e1c2-4>
Title: FirstResearch: Auditable Question Formation for LLM Scientific Discovery Agents
Snippet: Autonomous research agents. The AI Scientist is one of the earliest endto-end demonstrations of autonomous machine-learning research, combining idea generation, code execution, experiment analysis, paper writing, and simulated review (Lu et al., 2024). AI Scientist-v2 further develops this line with agentic tree search, reduced reliance on human-authored templates, and workshop-level autonomous manuscript generation (Yamada et al., 2025). These systems evaluate research agents through downstream artifacts such as papers, experiments, and reviewer scores. 

Agent Laboratory frames research automation as a staged assistant workflow: literature review, experimentation, and report writing (Schmidgall et al., 2025). This design highlights the practical value of structured research processes and human feedback, but its primary unit is a complete research workflow rather than the derivation quality of the initial research question. 

FirstResearch is complementary: it focuses on the question-formation layer that can feed into workflow systems. 

AI co-scientist is closest to our ideation setting because it focuses on hypothesis generation using generation, debate, ranking, and evolution (Gottweis et al., 2025). We adopt this as a strong baseline pattern and also test a small combination pilot that inserts co-scientist-style debate before certification. The key difference is that FirstResearch does not rely primarily on search over hypotheses; it forces each candidate to expose primitive assumptions, mechanism, tension, and falsifying test. 

Automated scientific discovery and hypothesis formation. Automated scientific discovery predates recent LLM agents. Literature-based discovery showed that useful hypotheses can arise by connecting separately published fragments of knowledge, as in Swanson's fish-oil and Raynaud's syndrome example (Swanson, 1986). Robot Scientist Adam demonstrated a more closed-loop form of automation in which a system generated hypotheses, designed experiments, executed them, and analyzed results in yeast functional genomics (King et al., 2009). These systems emphasize that scientific automation is not only about producing text; it is about maintaining a structured relation among hypothesis, evidence, experiment, and revision. Title: Embodied Science: Closing the Discovery Loop with Agentic Embodied AI
Snippet: Language-heavy, action-light (physically disembodied)   36,37 End-to-end research in silico e.g., AI Scientist 38 ; Kosmos 39 Action-heavy, language-light (cognitively shallow) 21,22 • Reliable embodied execution, but limited language-level reasoning and hypothesis formation; operate on raw instrument signals, rely primarily on heuristic or statistical decision-making, and enable direct interaction with the physical world. However, these systems are typically cognitively shallow: while they excel at executing experiments, they lack the capacity for mechanism-aware reasoning and hypothesis-driven inquiry. 

At one end of the execution-centric spectrum are single-step, instrument-bound systems. Automated liquid handlers, robotic pipetting platforms, and weighing systems exemplify this class. They automate isolated experimental operations with high precision and repeatability, yet each action is executed independently of the broader scientific context. Consequently, these systems constitute the basic infrastructure of automated experimentation: they robustly perform prescribed single-step actions, yet lack the capacity to analyze outcomes, reason about experimental context, or adapt behavior beyond explicit instructions. A more advanced, yet still execution-bound subclass extends automation to multi-step, protocol-driven execution. Platforms such as the Chemputer 40 and FLUID 40 encode experimental procedures as machine-executable workflows, enabling the automated realization of complex, multi-stage protocols. Compared to single-step systems, this approach extends automation from isolated actions to coordinated, multi-stage experimental execution. Although execution now spans multiple stages, the system does not analyze intermediate outcomes, reason about experimental context, or deviate from the prescribed workflow when unexpected results occur. At the most integrated end of execution-centric systems are closed-loop, feedback-driven platforms, including A-Lab 42 , RoboChem 43 , and CRESt 44 . By integrating robotic execution with online characterization and statistical optimization methods, including Bayesian optimization and evolutionary search, these platforms demonstrate impressive autonomy over extended experimental campaigns, adapting parameters in response to observed outcomes and achieving local optimization in high-dimensional spaces. However, the closed loop operates primarily at the level of numerical feedback rather than scientific representation.
</snippet>

Title: From Prompts to Protocols: An AI Agent for Laboratory Automation
Snippet: Automating science laboratories enables faster, safer, more accurate, and more reproducible execution of protocols, accelerating the discovery and testing of new materials, drugs, and more. However, setting up and running autonomous labs requires coordinating numerous instruments and robots, forcing scientists to write code, manage configuration files, and navigate complex software infrastructure. We present an AI agent architecture that integrates large language models with laboratory orchestration, enabling scientists to interactively create and monitor automated lab protocols using natural language. Integrated into the Experiment Orchestration System (EOS), the AI agent operates under an agentic loop with automated validation and error correction, and supports the complete experimental lifecycle: creating protocols, running and monitoring both protocols and closed-loop optimization campaigns, and analyzing results. A visual graph editor renders protocols as interactive node-based diagrams synchronized with the AI agent's protocol representation, enabling seamless alternation between AI-assisted and manual protocol construction. Evaluated on three simulated automated labs spanning chemistry, biology, and materials science, the AI agent achieves a 97% first-attempt protocol generation success rate and an order of magnitude reduction in required interface actions.
</snippet>

Title: From Prompts to Protocols: An AI Agent for Laboratory Automation
Snippet: Laboratory automation can accelerate the discovery and testing of new materials, drugs, and other products by enabling scientists to run protocols faster, more safely, more accurately, and with greater reproducibility [1], [2], [3]. Lab automation can range from automating a single instrument to coordinating complex multi-step protocols across distributed laboratories [1]. Setting up and running autonomous labs typically requires coordinating numerous instruments and robots, which must be scheduled and operated to complete experiments. To support this coordination, autonomous labs often use laboratory orchestration software that provides scientists with standard interfaces for defining and executing multi-step protocols. Orchestrators can automatically schedule when and on what instruments tasks run, manage connectivity to diverse lab hardware, collect and organize data from protocol runs, and provide frameworks to optimize protocol parameters [4], [5], [6]. However, creating and monitoring protocols using laboratory orchestration software remains tedious. Scientists must often implement code using Python or visual block-based programming, author configuration files, understand scheduling semantics, and monitor execution across multiple subsystems. These tedious steps, for which chemists and other physical scientists currently receive little training, serve as a barrier to adoption of lab automation [1]. 

In this paper, we present an AI agent architecture that integrates large language models with laboratory orchestration, enabling scientists to interactively create and monitor automated protocols using natural language. The AI agent, powered by state-of-the-art large language models, enables scientists to create protocols, submit protocols for execution, monitor protocol runs, run optimization campaigns with these protocols, and query and analyze generated data, all without writing code or configuration files. For example, a scientist can ask the AI agent to "add 10mL of each of the three input reagents into the flask, mix using a magnetic mixer for 20s, and characterize the solution using mass spectrometry", and the AI agent generates a complete, validated protocol (represented by a directed acyclic graph of tasks and associated parameters) by reasoning about available devices, implemented task capabilities, and laboratory constraints. 

We integrated this AI agent into the Experiment Orchestration System (EOS), a laboratory orchestration software supporting protocol creation and monitoring [4].
</snippet>

Title: Experiment-as-Code Labs: A Declarative Stack for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery
Snippet: Autonomous laboratories. Existing laboratory automation software, such as LIMS and ELNs, can automate individual components of experimental workflows, including sample tracking, instrument control, data capture, and scheduling, to improve efficiency and traceability (MaterialsZone, 2024;LabLynx, 2025;STARLIMS, 2025). However, these systems typically do not support end-to-end experimental execution. Moreover, experiments are commonly encoded as GUI-driven workflows or vendor-specific configuration templates that are tightly coupled to a single platform's instrument library and data schema. While these representations expose a declarative interface at the surface level, they are not portable, statically checkable, or composable across labs: they describe which buttons to click in which tool rather than what experiment to perform, leading to siloed ecosystems that evolve slowly and continue to require substantial human effort for experimental implementation, verification, and day-to-day operation (MaterialsZone, 2024;Scispot, 2026;Holland, 2020). In contrast, EaC envisions a well-typed, lab-independent program over a standardized resource model, with explicit dependencies, capability schemas, and execution semantics that admit static validation, deterministic compilation, and cross-site execution. These limitations have motivated the emergence of autonomous and "cloud" laboratories (e.g., Emerald Cloud Lab (Emerald Cloud Lab, 2025)), which provide remotely accessible, highly automated facilities that allow researchers to configure, execute, and analyze experiments through centralized software interfaces without being physically present. By offering on-demand access to specialized and expensive equipment, these platforms draw analogies to cloud computing infrastructures in the goal of lowering the barrier to conducting complex experiments (Arias, 2024). However, as the number of instruments and analytical capabilities grows, configuring experiments increasingly resembles orchestrating many cloud services, imposing steep learning curves and exposing users to imperative, low-level interfaces that remain cumbersome and error-prone, ultimately limiting the efficiency gains of laboratory automation in practice. 

National and international initiatives. Recent policy frameworks worldwide have advocated the integration of AI with scientific infrastructure, recognizing automation as a strategic imperative for accelerating discovery.

Title: AutoResearch AI: Towards AI-Powered Research Automation for Scientific Discovery
Snippet: Early anchors such as Robot Scientist Adam [64] and AI Feynman [65] showed that selected components of discovery could be automated in structured settings, such as automated hypothesis testing, symbolic recovery, or reasoning over constrained scientific spaces, while broader discussions on the Automation of Science [61] framed automation as a workflow-level question. With the rise of language models, systems such as BioPlanner [49] and LitLLM [15] moved this layer toward protocol reasoning and literature-centered research support. In 2024, retrieval-and synthesis-oriented systems including Research Agent [50], STORM [66], OpenScholar [16], SciSage [67], HypER [48], and PaperQA2 [17] made grounded search, multi-perspective synthesis, hypothesis support, and paper-grounded answering part of stable assistant workflows. STORM, for example, is explicitly a retrieval-and multi-perspective-questioning system for grounded long-form writing rather than an executional research agent • L2-S: Single-step automated execution. The next historical transition occurred when AI systems began to execute bounded scientific operations rather than only support knowledge work. We describe this regime as L2-S, or single-step automated execution. Systems in this layer can carry out well-specified operations such as tool invocation, code execution, protocol enactment, laboratory control, model training, data-driven analysis, or bounded experimental support. Coscientist [71] connected language models to search, code execution, laboratory documentation, and experimental automation in chemistry, while A-Lab [72] demonstrated autonomous materials synthesis through computation, historical or literature-derived knowledge, active learning, and robotic execution. Both works expanded executional capacity, but in controlled scientific domains rather than in general research workflows. In 2024, CycleResearcher [73], MLR-Copilot [74], RD Agent [75], AIGS [76], and Virtual Lab [77] extended bounded execution into planning, implementation, revision, and virtual experimental environments. The defining property of this layer is not full workflow autonomy, but the transfer of selected executable tasks from humans to AI under constrained goals, controlled settings, and external verification. 

• L2-I: Interactive workflow automation.

Context and counterfactual

Title: Idea2Story: An Automated Pipeline for Transforming Research Concepts into Complete Scientific Narratives
Snippet: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have driven growing interest in autonomous scientific discovery agents that aim to automate the full research lifecycle, from code generation to experimental execution (Hu et al., 2026;Zhang et al., 2025a;Lin et al., 2025). Early systems such as The AI Scientist (v1) (Lu et al., 2024) demonstrate the viability of end-to-end automation but rely heavily on manually crafted code templates and largely linear exploration workflows, which restrict discovery depth and adaptability. Later approaches, including The AI Scientist-v2 (Yamada et al., 2025) and Kosmos (Mitchener et al., 2025), reduce reliance on explicit template through the incorporation of agentic tree search and experiment management agents, enabling iterative and multi-round exploration. 

In research ideation, LLM-generated ideas are often perceived as highly novel during initial screening; however, prior studies (Si et al., 2024) uncover a critical paradox whereby such ideas tend to underperform after implementation relative to human-generated ideas, indicating limited feasibility and practical utility. As more ideas are generated, LLM outputs exhibit growing similarity, leading to diminished meaningful diversity. Similar limitations have also been observed in research evaluation and peer review (Liang et al., 2024;Xu et al., 2025;Thakkar et al., 2025;Zhang et al., 2026). Existing AI-based reviewers display systematic blind spots: Shin et al. (2025) shows that LLM reviewers place disproportionate emphasis on technical correctness while undervaluing novelty, deviating from human expert judgment, while Sahu et al. (2025) demonstrates that AI reviewers struggle to distinguish fine-grained acceptance categories and are susceptible to sycophancy, with review scores increasing unreasonably after exposure to author rebuttals. Although recent approaches such as AgentReview (Jin et al., 2024) seek to mitigate these deficiencies by simulating diverse reviewer roles, automated evaluation systems remain less reliable than human experts in identifying robust accept/reject decision boundaries.

Title: The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search
Snippet: AI is increasingly playing a pivotal role in transforming how scientific discoveries are made. We introduce The AI Scientist-v2, an end-to-end agentic system capable of producing the first entirely AI generated peer-review-accepted workshop paper. This system iteratively formulates scientific hypotheses, designs and executes experiments, analyzes and visualizes data, and autonomously authors scientific manuscripts. Compared to its predecessor (v1, Lu et al., 2024 arXiv:2408.06292), The AI Scientist-v2 eliminates the reliance on human-authored code templates, generalizes effectively across diverse machine learning domains, and leverages a novel progressive agentic tree-search methodology managed by a dedicated experiment manager agent. Additionally, we enhance the AI reviewer component by integrating a Vision-Language Model (VLM) feedback loop for iterative refinement of content and aesthetics of the figures. We evaluated The AI Scientist-v2 by submitting three fully autonomous manuscripts to a peer-reviewed ICLR workshop. Notably, one manuscript achieved high enough scores to exceed the average human acceptance threshold, marking the first instance of a fully AI-generated paper successfully navigating a peer review. This accomplishment highlights the growing capability of AI in conducting all aspects of scientific research. We anticipate that further advancements in autonomous scientific discovery technologies will profoundly impact human knowledge generation, enabling unprecedented scalability in research productivity and significantly accelerating scientific breakthroughs, greatly benefiting society at large. We have open-sourced the code at https://github.com/SakanaAI/AI-Scientist-v2 to foster the future development of this transformative technology. We also discuss the role of AI in science, including AI safety.

Title: Learning the ARTS of Search for Automated Discovery
Snippet: Scientific discovery is an iterative search process in which multiple hypotheses are proposed, tested, and refined to arrive at novel insights. The advent of large reasoning models have led to their use as AI Scientist conducting this search [36,31]. In the past, these systems have produced new constructions in extremal combinatorics [51], improved classical algorithms for matrix multiplication [39], planned and executed autonomous chemical syntheses [4], and generated novel hypotheses on antimicrobial resistance [15]. The success of these systems often rely on large sampling budgets and repeated execution of expensive experiments [51,39]. This cost is significant in ML research [50,38,7,53], where each hypothesis must be implemented as code, trained, debugged, and evaluated. Scaling automated research, therefore, requires efficient searching algorithms. 

Existing search algorithms fall into three categories: linear search, tree-based search, and evolutionary search. Searching linearly [38,20,31] makes it difficult for the agent to revisit and improve upon an initial bad hypothesis [42]. Tree-based [50,22,9,34,8] and evolutionary [39,44,33,52] algorithms alleviate this concern, but they search using score-based heuristics. This conflates hypothesis quality with it's execution in code. In such methods, a modest hypothesis that is well implemented is likely to be preferred over a promising hypothesis with preliminary execution. For instance, an Figure 1: A single search step of ARTS. A node is one validated experiment with a hypothesis, code, logs, and score. Starting from the current search tree (Tree to expand), the scientist inspects the candidate nodes and reasons about why each scored as it did, then selects the most promising node rather than the one with the highest score. In this figure, it picks the node with score 0.10 since the low score comes from under training rather than a weak hypothesis (Node selection). Through verbalized sampling the scientist then proposes diverse hypotheses with probabilities and samples one, which the executor implements, runs, and scores (Node expansion). The resulting node (0.55) becomes the new best and is added to the tree.

Title: GUIDE: Towards Scalable Advising for Research Ideas
Snippet: Our work lies at the intersection of scientific hypothesis verification, automated peer review, and modular AI scientist systems. Departing from approaches that produce surface-level critiques or aim for full-lifecycle coverage, we present a focused, retrieval-augmented, rubric-aligned system that generates structured, high-fidelity scientific feedback.

Title: AI Scientists Fail Without Strong Implementation Capability
Snippet: The fundamental bottleneck for AI Scientists lies in their implementation capability to effectively execute the verification of these ideas. 

We defend our argument by analyzing quantitative evidence from existing benchmarks used to evaluate LLMs' abilities in performing complex engineering tasks (Section 3.2). While LLMs can generate highly novel ideas (Si et al., 2024, Chai et al., 2024, Gottweis et al., 2025), their performance in experiment execution is exceptionally poor (Table 1). For instance, a leading LLM like Claude 3.5 Sonnet scored only 1.8% on PaperBench (Starace et al., 2025). This implementation gap is further supported by a systematic evaluation (Section 3.3), which leverages a state-of-the-art review model, DeepReviewer-14B (Zhu et al., 2025), to assess 28 research papers generated by five advanced AI Scientist systems. The results demonstrate that current AI Scientist systems lack the execution capabilities needed to execute rigorous experiments and produce high-quality scientific papers. Finally, to clearly illustrate the root cause of the implementation gap, we provide an in-depth discussion on the fundamental limitations of AI Scientist (Section 4). 

In summary, this paper validates and deeply analyzes the implementation gap in existing AI Scientist systems based on extensive quantitative evidence and a simulated peer-review process. Furthermore, as the development of AI Scientists will bring greater regulatory challenges, we comprehensively examine the ethical considerations (Section 5) faced by AI Scientists and suggest directions for future research (Section 6). We hope this position paper will contribute to a clearer understanding of the limitations of current AI Scientist, shedding light on the future development of AI Scientist.

Title: The More You Automate, the Less You See: Hidden Pitfalls of AI Scientist Systems
Snippet: Automating the scientific enterprise has been an explicit research goal of computational and AI researchers for several decades [KRO + 09, SAB + 10, YLN22]. For instance, King et al. [KRO + 09] demonstrated the feasibility of fully automated systems for generating and testing scientific hypotheses, exemplified by the "Robot Scientist" capable of independently identifying functional genes in yeast metabolism. Sparkes et al. 

[SAB + 10] further advanced this line of work by integrating automated reasoning and laboratory robotics, aiming for autonomous scientific discovery with minimal human intervention. The advent of LLMs, along with their multimodal variants and agent-based extensions, has led to a surge in the development of automated scientist systems. We summarize several representative state-of-the-art systems in Table 1. 

There are different types of AI scientist systems, including those that are claimed to fully automate scientific discovery [LLL + 24, YLL + 25] and those designed to assist human scientists in their research [SSW + 25, Aut25, TZF + 25, Int25, GCM + 25]. Among the fully automated systems, The AI Scientist v1 [LLL + 24] is one of the earliest attempts to integrate the entire scientific pipeline: idea generation, code writing based on fixed templates, experiment execution, result visualization, manuscript drafting, and even simulated peer review. However, its reliance on pre-specified code templates and limited experiment management restricted flexibility. The AI Scientist v2 [YLL + 25] further eliminates the need for templates and introduces a treesearch-based experiment manager for more systematic exploration and incorporation of Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based feedback in the review stage. 

In contrast, in the case of AI assistants such as Carl [Aut25] and Zochi [Int25], human oversight is integral. Human experts must verify outputs at three checkpoints-transitioning from ideation to experimentation, from experimentation to presentation, and after presentation-before further progress is permitted. Agent Laboratory [SSW + 25] is designed to assist human scientists in executing their research ideas while allowing flexible levels of human involvement, where users can choose to provide feedback at any stage of scientific research.

Title: FirstResearch: Auditable Question Formation for LLM Scientific Discovery Agents
Snippet: Autonomous research agents. The AI Scientist is one of the earliest endto-end demonstrations of autonomous machine-learning research, combining idea generation, code execution, experiment analysis, paper writing, and simulated review (Lu et al., 2024). AI Scientist-v2 further develops this line with agentic tree search, reduced reliance on human-authored templates, and workshop-level autonomous manuscript generation (Yamada et al., 2025). These systems evaluate research agents through downstream artifacts such as papers, experiments, and reviewer scores. 

Agent Laboratory frames research automation as a staged assistant workflow: literature review, experimentation, and report writing (Schmidgall et al., 2025). This design highlights the practical value of structured research processes and human feedback, but its primary unit is a complete research workflow rather than the derivation quality of the initial research question. 

FirstResearch is complementary: it focuses on the question-formation layer that can feed into workflow systems. 

AI co-scientist is closest to our ideation setting because it focuses on hypothesis generation using generation, debate, ranking, and evolution (Gottweis et al., 2025). We adopt this as a strong baseline pattern and also test a small combination pilot that inserts co-scientist-style debate before certification. The key difference is that FirstResearch does not rely primarily on search over hypotheses; it forces each candidate to expose primitive assumptions, mechanism, tension, and falsifying test. 

Automated scientific discovery and hypothesis formation. Automated scientific discovery predates recent LLM agents. Literature-based discovery showed that useful hypotheses can arise by connecting separately published fragments of knowledge, as in Swanson's fish-oil and Raynaud's syndrome example (Swanson, 1986). Robot Scientist Adam demonstrated a more closed-loop form of automation in which a system generated hypotheses, designed experiments, executed them, and analyzed results in yeast functional genomics (King et al., 2009). These systems emphasize that scientific automation is not only about producing text; it is about maintaining a structured relation among hypothesis, evidence, experiment, and revision. FirstResearch inherits this structured-science view but targets an earlier bottleneck: making the derivation of a proposed research question inspectable before execution.

snippet.text:
Automating the scientific enterprise has been an explicit research goal of computational and AI researchers for several decades [KRO + 09, SAB + 10, YLN22]. For instance, King et al. [KRO + 09] demonstrated the feasibility of fully automated systems for generating and testing scientific hypotheses, exemplified by the "Robot Scientist" capable of independently identifying functional genes in yeast metabolism. Sparkes et al. 

[SAB + 10] further advanced this line of work by integrating automated reasoning and laboratory robotics, aiming for autonomous scientific discovery with minimal human intervention. The advent of LLMs, along with their multimodal variants and agent-based extensions, has led to a surge in the development of automated scientist systems. We summarize several representative state-of-the-art systems in Table 1. 

There are different types of AI scientist systems, including those that are claimed to fully automate scientific discovery [LLL + 24, YLL + 25] and those designed to assist human scientists in their research [SSW + 25, Aut25, TZF + 25, Int25, GCM + 25]. Among the fully automated systems, The AI Scientist v1 [LLL + 24] is one of the earliest attempts to integrate the entire scientific pipeline: idea generation, code writing based on fixed templates, experiment execution, result visualization, manuscript drafting, and even simulated peer review. However, its reliance on pre-specified code templates and limited experiment management restricted flexibility. The AI Scientist v2 [YLL + 25] further eliminates the need for templates and introduces a treesearch-based experiment manager for more systematic exploration and incorporation of Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based feedback in the review stage. 

In contrast, in the case of AI assistants such as Carl [Aut25] and Zochi [Int25], human oversight is integral. Human experts must verify outputs at three checkpoints-transitioning from ideation to experimentation, from experimentation to presentation, and after presentation-before further progress is permitted. Agent Laboratory [SSW + 25] is designed to assist human scientists in executing their research ideas while allowing flexible levels of human involvement, where users can choose to provide feedback at any stage of scientific research.

snippet.text:
Autonomous research agents. The AI Scientist is one of the earliest endto-end demonstrations of autonomous machine-learning research, combining idea generation, code execution, experiment analysis, paper writing, and simulated review (Lu et al., 2024). AI Scientist-v2 further develops this line with agentic tree search, reduced reliance on human-authored templates, and workshop-level autonomous manuscript generation (Yamada et al., 2025). These systems evaluate research agents through downstream artifacts such as papers, experiments, and reviewer scores. 

Agent Laboratory frames research automation as a staged assistant workflow: literature review, experimentation, and report writing (Schmidgall et al., 2025). This design highlights the practical value of structured research processes and human feedback, but its primary unit is a complete research workflow rather than the derivation quality of the initial research question. 

FirstResearch is complementary: it focuses on the question-formation layer that can feed into workflow systems. 

AI co-scientist is closest to our ideation setting because it focuses on hypothesis generation using generation, debate, ranking, and evolution (Gottweis et al., 2025). We adopt this as a strong baseline pattern and also test a small combination pilot that inserts co-scientist-style debate before certification. The key difference is that FirstResearch does not rely primarily on search over hypotheses; it forces each candidate to expose primitive assumptions, mechanism, tension, and falsifying test. 

Automated scientific discovery and hypothesis formation. Automated scientific discovery predates recent LLM agents. Literature-based discovery showed that useful hypotheses can arise by connecting separately published fragments of knowledge, as in Swanson's fish-oil and Raynaud's syndrome example (Swanson, 1986). Robot Scientist Adam demonstrated a more closed-loop form of automation in which a system generated hypotheses, designed experiments, executed them, and analyzed results in yeast functional genomics (King et al., 2009). These systems emphasize that scientific automation is not only about producing text; it is about maintaining a structured relation among hypothesis, evidence, experiment, and revision. FirstResearch inherits this structured-science view but targets an earlier bottleneck: making the derivation of a proposed research question inspectable before execution.

documents.title: AI Scientists Fail Without Strong Implementation Capability
documents.snippet:
The fundamental bottleneck for AI Scientists lies in their implementation capability to effectively execute the verification of these ideas. 

We defend our argument by analyzing quantitative evidence from existing benchmarks used to evaluate LLMs' abilities in performing complex engineering tasks (Section 3.2). While LLMs can generate highly novel ideas (Si et al., 2024, Chai et al., 2024, Gottweis et al., 2025), their performance in experiment execution is exceptionally poor (Table 1). For instance, a leading LLM like Claude 3.5 Sonnet scored only 1.8% on PaperBench (Starace et al., 2025). This implementation gap is further supported by a systematic evaluation (Section 3.3), which leverages a state-of-the-art review model, DeepReviewer-14B (Zhu et al., 2025), to assess 28 research papers generated by five advanced AI Scientist systems. The results demonstrate that current AI Scientist systems lack the execution capabilities needed to execute rigorous experiments and produce high-quality scientific papers. Finally, to clearly illustrate the root cause of the implementation gap, we provide an in-depth discussion on the fundamental limitations of AI Scientist (Section 4). 

In summary, this paper validates and deeply analyzes the implementation gap in existing AI Scientist systems based on extensive quantitative evidence and a simulated peer-review process. Furthermore, as the development of AI Scientists will bring greater regulatory challenges, we comprehensively examine the ethical considerations (Section 5) faced by AI Scientists and suggest directions for future research (Section 6). We hope this position paper will contribute to a clearer understanding of the limitations of current AI Scientist, shedding light on the future development of AI Scientist.

Title: Embodied Science: Closing the Discovery Loop with Agentic Embodied AI
Snippet: Language-heavy, action-light (physically disembodied)   36,37 End-to-end research in silico e.g., AI Scientist 38 ; Kosmos 39 Action-heavy, language-light (cognitively shallow) 21,22 • Reliable embodied execution, but limited language-level reasoning and hypothesis formation; operate on raw instrument signals, rely primarily on heuristic or statistical decision-making, and enable direct interaction with the physical world. However, these systems are typically cognitively shallow: while they excel at executing experiments, they lack the capacity for mechanism-aware reasoning and hypothesis-driven inquiry. 

At one end of the execution-centric spectrum are single-step, instrument-bound systems. Automated liquid handlers, robotic pipetting platforms, and weighing systems exemplify this class. They automate isolated experimental operations with high precision and repeatability, yet each action is executed independently of the broader scientific context. Consequently, these systems constitute the basic infrastructure of automated experimentation: they robustly perform prescribed single-step actions, yet lack the capacity to analyze outcomes, reason about experimental context, or adapt behavior beyond explicit instructions. A more advanced, yet still execution-bound subclass extends automation to multi-step, protocol-driven execution. Platforms such as the Chemputer 40 and FLUID 40 encode experimental procedures as machine-executable workflows, enabling the automated realization of complex, multi-stage protocols. Compared to single-step systems, this approach extends automation from isolated actions to coordinated, multi-stage experimental execution. Although execution now spans multiple stages, the system does not analyze intermediate outcomes, reason about experimental context, or deviate from the prescribed workflow when unexpected results occur. At the most integrated end of execution-centric systems are closed-loop, feedback-driven platforms, including A-Lab 42 , RoboChem 43 , and CRESt 44 . By integrating robotic execution with online characterization and statistical optimization methods, including Bayesian optimization and evolutionary search, these platforms demonstrate impressive autonomy over extended experimental campaigns, adapting parameters in response to observed outcomes and achieving local optimization in high-dimensional spaces. However, the closed loop operates primarily at the level of numerical feedback rather than scientific representation.

Title: From Prompts to Protocols: An AI Agent for Laboratory Automation
Snippet: Automating science laboratories enables faster, safer, more accurate, and more reproducible execution of protocols, accelerating the discovery and testing of new materials, drugs, and more. However, setting up and running autonomous labs requires coordinating numerous instruments and robots, forcing scientists to write code, manage configuration files, and navigate complex software infrastructure. We present an AI agent architecture that integrates large language models with laboratory orchestration, enabling scientists to interactively create and monitor automated lab protocols using natural language. Integrated into the Experiment Orchestration System (EOS), the AI agent operates under an agentic loop with automated validation and error correction, and supports the complete experimental lifecycle: creating protocols, running and monitoring both protocols and closed-loop optimization campaigns, and analyzing results. A visual graph editor renders protocols as interactive node-based diagrams synchronized with the AI agent's protocol representation, enabling seamless alternation between AI-assisted and manual protocol construction. Evaluated on three simulated automated labs spanning chemistry, biology, and materials science, the AI agent achieves a 97% first-attempt protocol generation success rate and an order of magnitude reduction in required interface actions.

Title: From Prompts to Protocols: An AI Agent for Laboratory Automation
Snippet: Laboratory automation can accelerate the discovery and testing of new materials, drugs, and other products by enabling scientists to run protocols faster, more safely, more accurately, and with greater reproducibility [1], [2], [3]. Lab automation can range from automating a single instrument to coordinating complex multi-step protocols across distributed laboratories [1]. Setting up and running autonomous labs typically requires coordinating numerous instruments and robots, which must be scheduled and operated to complete experiments. To support this coordination, autonomous labs often use laboratory orchestration software that provides scientists with standard interfaces for defining and executing multi-step protocols. Orchestrators can automatically schedule when and on what instruments tasks run, manage connectivity to diverse lab hardware, collect and organize data from protocol runs, and provide frameworks to optimize protocol parameters [4], [5], [6]. However, creating and monitoring protocols using laboratory orchestration software remains tedious. Scientists must often implement code using Python or visual block-based programming, author configuration files, understand scheduling semantics, and monitor execution across multiple subsystems. These tedious steps, for which chemists and other physical scientists currently receive little training, serve as a barrier to adoption of lab automation [1]. 

In this paper, we present an AI agent architecture that integrates large language models with laboratory orchestration, enabling scientists to interactively create and monitor automated protocols using natural language. The AI agent, powered by state-of-the-art large language models, enables scientists to create protocols, submit protocols for execution, monitor protocol runs, run optimization campaigns with these protocols, and query and analyze generated data, all without writing code or configuration files. For example, a scientist can ask the AI agent to "add 10mL of each of the three input reagents into the flask, mix using a magnetic mixer for 20s, and characterize the solution using mass spectrometry", and the AI agent generates a complete, validated protocol (represented by a directed acyclic graph of tasks and associated parameters) by reasoning about available devices, implemented task capabilities, and laboratory constraints. 

We integrated this AI agent into the Experiment Orchestration System (EOS), a laboratory orchestration software supporting protocol creation and monitoring [4].

Title: Experiment-as-Code Labs: A Declarative Stack for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery
Snippet: Autonomous laboratories. Existing laboratory automation software, such as LIMS and ELNs, can automate individual components of experimental workflows, including sample tracking, instrument control, data capture, and scheduling, to improve efficiency and traceability (MaterialsZone, 2024;LabLynx, 2025;STARLIMS, 2025). However, these systems typically do not support end-to-end experimental execution. Moreover, experiments are commonly encoded as GUI-driven workflows or vendor-specific configuration templates that are tightly coupled to a single platform's instrument library and data schema. While these representations expose a declarative interface at the surface level, they are not portable, statically checkable, or composable across labs: they describe which buttons to click in which tool rather than what experiment to perform, leading to siloed ecosystems that evolve slowly and continue to require substantial human effort for experimental implementation, verification, and day-to-day operation (MaterialsZone, 2024;Scispot, 2026;Holland, 2020). In contrast, EaC envisions a well-typed, lab-independent program over a standardized resource model, with explicit dependencies, capability schemas, and execution semantics that admit static validation, deterministic compilation, and cross-site execution. These limitations have motivated the emergence of autonomous and "cloud" laboratories (e.g., Emerald Cloud Lab (Emerald Cloud Lab, 2025)), which provide remotely accessible, highly automated facilities that allow researchers to configure, execute, and analyze experiments through centralized software interfaces without being physically present. By offering on-demand access to specialized and expensive equipment, these platforms draw analogies to cloud computing infrastructures in the goal of lowering the barrier to conducting complex experiments (Arias, 2024). However, as the number of instruments and analytical capabilities grows, configuring experiments increasingly resembles orchestrating many cloud services, imposing steep learning curves and exposing users to imperative, low-level interfaces that remain cumbersome and error-prone, ultimately limiting the efficiency gains of laboratory automation in practice. 

National and international initiatives. Recent policy frameworks worldwide have advocated the integration of AI with scientific infrastructure, recognizing automation as a strategic imperative for accelerating discovery.

Title: AutoResearch AI: Towards AI-Powered Research Automation for Scientific Discovery
Snippet: Early anchors such as Robot Scientist Adam [64] and AI Feynman [65] showed that selected components of discovery could be automated in structured settings, such as automated hypothesis testing, symbolic recovery, or reasoning over constrained scientific spaces, while broader discussions on the Automation of Science [61] framed automation as a workflow-level question. With the rise of language models, systems such as BioPlanner [49] and LitLLM [15] moved this layer toward protocol reasoning and literature-centered research support. In 2024, retrieval-and synthesis-oriented systems including Research Agent [50], STORM [66], OpenScholar [16], SciSage [67], HypER [48], and PaperQA2 [17] made grounded search, multi-perspective synthesis, hypothesis support, and paper-grounded answering part of stable assistant workflows. STORM, for example, is explicitly a retrieval-and multi-perspective-questioning system for grounded long-form writing rather than an executional research agent • L2-S: Single-step automated execution. The next historical transition occurred when AI systems began to execute bounded scientific operations rather than only support knowledge work. We describe this regime as L2-S, or single-step automated execution. Systems in this layer can carry out well-specified operations such as tool invocation, code execution, protocol enactment, laboratory control, model training, data-driven analysis, or bounded experimental support. Coscientist [71] connected language models to search, code execution, laboratory documentation, and experimental automation in chemistry, while A-Lab [72] demonstrated autonomous materials synthesis through computation, historical or literature-derived knowledge, active learning, and robotic execution. Both works expanded executional capacity, but in controlled scientific domains rather than in general research workflows. In 2024, CycleResearcher [73], MLR-Copilot [74], RD Agent [75], AIGS [76], and Virtual Lab [77] extended bounded execution into planning, implementation, revision, and virtual experimental environments. The defining property of this layer is not full workflow autonomy, but the transfer of selected executable tasks from humans to AI under constrained goals, controlled settings, and external verification. 

• L2-I: Interactive workflow automation.
